assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide about a job offer in Denver. She could take it, or she could stay in her hometown and finish her nursing degree. It was a hard choice and she was worried about it. She asked her mother first. Her mother said right away, "Stay. Family is here." If Dana had stopped asking there, she would have stayed. Instead she kept asking, and that is why her choice turned out good. I think asking more than one person helps you make a great decision, because it shows you blind spots, gives you different kinds of knowledge, and helps you understand your own reasons.

The first good thing is that every adviser has a bias. Dana's mother loves her and wanted her close, which is a sweet reason, but it was partly about the mother's feelings. Then Dana asked her friend Marcus, who moved away for work years ago. He said leaving was the best thing he ever did, and he was happy about it. His view came from his own life too. Neither of them was lying and both were kind. Each one just told the story they lived. When Dana heard both, she could see where the advice came from. One opinion looks like a fact. Two opinions that disagree look like what they are, which is a point of view.

The second benefit is that different people know different things. Dana also talked to her nursing instructor, who is a wonderful teacher and a smart person. The instructor saw something nobody else saw. The Denver job was in billing instead of patient care, and leaving school early would make it hard to come back to the work Dana loves. Dana was excited about the nice salary, but she forgot to think about five years later. That was a bad mistake waiting to happen. Her instructor had watched many students make the same jump and knew how it ended. Her mother and Marcus love Dana, but they do not work in nursing, so they could not give her that fact. One adviser, even a caring one, only holds one piece of the puzzle.

Third, talking to several people makes you explain your problem again and again, and explaining is a great way to think. By the third talk, Dana heard herself say the same thing every time. She wanted to finish her program. What she wanted most was to feel like she was going somewhere. Each person asked a different question, and each question helped her find what mattered most. Sometimes the best part of advice is the question it gives you. When Marcus asked, "What would you regret more?" she knew right away. Quitting her degree would feel awful, much worse than turning down a job.

Of course, there is a limit. Too many voices can be confusing, and someone who asks ten people might only be hunting for a person to say what she wants to hear. That is not a good plan. You should not just count votes. Dana did not follow the crowd. She looked at the reasons behind each view. A smart rule is to ask a few people with different jobs and different lives, then look at their reasons.

In the end, Dana stayed and finished her degree. It was not easy, and she was tired and stressed for a while. However, she got a good job at a hospital, and she was proud. Her mother was right about waiting, Marcus was right about moving, and her instructor was right about timing. That is why asking more people is a smart move. It won't fix every problem, and it isn't always fun, but a choice built on many honest voices is a strong choice. I am glad Dana had good people to trust.
essay_2:
Last spring my cousin Dana had to choose between two things. She could take a job in Denver or stay home and finish her nursing degree. She asked her mom first, and her mom said right away, "Stay. Your family is here." If Dana had stopped asking right there, she probably would have stayed. But she kept asking other people, and I think that is a big reason things worked out for her. Asking more than one person for advice helps you make a better choice because you find out what you were missing, you hear from people who know different things, and you have to figure out what you really want.

The first reason is that everybody who gives advice has a bias, so when you ask a few people the biases kind of cancel out. Dana's mom wanted her to stay because she would miss her. That does not mean her advice was bad, but part of it was about her mom's feelings. Then Dana asked her friend Marcus, who moved away for work a long time ago. He told her leaving was the best thing he ever did. His advice came from his own life too. Neither of them was lying, they were just telling what happened to them. When Dana heard both, she could see where each answer was coming from. If you only hear one opinion, it sounds like a fact. When two people disagree, you can tell they are just opinions.

The second reason is that different people know different things. Dana also talked to one of her nursing teachers, and the teacher brought up something her mom and Marcus never thought of. The job in Denver was in billing, not taking care of patients. If she quit school without her degree, it would be really hard to go back to nursing later. Dana was so excited about the money that she never thought about where the job would take her in five years. Her teacher had seen a lot of students do the same thing and knew how it usually went. Dana could not have got that from people who loved her but did not work in that field. One person, even a nice one, only knows a small piece of what you need to know.

The third reason is that when you ask a bunch of people, you have to explain your problem over and over, and explaining it makes you think. By the third time Dana told the story, she noticed she kept saying the same thing. She did not really want to leave her program. She just wanted to feel like she was getting somewhere. Every person asked her a little different question, and each one made her say what mattered most to her. Sometimes the best part of someone's advice is not their answer, it is the question they make you think about. Marcus asked her, "What would you regret more?" and she realized she would regret quitting her degree way more than saying no to a job.

Of course, asking people has limits. If you ask too many people it can get confusing, and someone who asks ten people might just be looking for one person to say what they already want to hear. It is not about counting votes. Dana did not just go with what most people said. She thought about the reasons behind what each person said. I think a good rule is to ask a few people who come from different places, and then look at why they think what they think instead of just what they picked.

In the end Dana stayed and finished her degree, and later she got a better job at a hospital in Denver. Her mom was right about waiting, Marcus was right about moving, and her teacher was right about the timing. Nobody had the whole picture, but all together they gave her enough of it to feel sure about her choice. That is why asking more than one person does not mean you have bad judgment. It makes your judgment stronger, because a decision based on a few honest opinions is a lot safer than one based on only one person.
